sections.text: The water intake calculator estimates your daily water target as 0.5 ounces per pound of body weight (about 33 mL per kilogram), plus a fixed amount for how active you are and a fixed amount for the climate you live or work in. A 150 lb person with a sedentary day in a temperate climate gets 75 oz (about 2.2 L). The same person with moderate exercise in a hot, humid climate gets 107 oz (about 3.2 L). It is a planning estimate, not a medical requirement, and the calculator itself says thirst and pale-yellow urine are better day-to-day guides than hitting an exact number.

The calculator adds three pieces: baseline ounces (body weight in pounds times 0.5), an activity adjustment, and a climate adjustment. Weights entered in kilograms are converted to pounds first. Ounces are converted to liters with 0.0295735 L per ounce, and the cups figure is total ounces divided by 8, always rounded up.
Worked example: one 150 lb adult, every activity and climate
Each cell shows total ounces and liters from the calculator's formula for a 150 lb adult, with liters rounded to one decimal place.

Because the activity and climate additions are fixed amounts, they matter more in proportion for smaller people. The hot-climate addition of 16 oz is 16% of a 200 lb person's 100 oz baseline, 21% of a 150 lb person's, and 27% of a 120 lb person's.
Does the target include water from food?

The calculator's note says the target already accounts for activity and climate, and that about 20% of daily fluid comes from food, so you do not need to drink every ounce. If you apply that assumption literally, a 75 oz target means roughly 60 oz from drinks, and a 107 oz target means roughly 86 oz. The 20% figure is the calculator's assumption and varies with diet. The National Academies report on dietary reference intakes sets adequate intakes for total water, covering drinking water, beverages and food together, which is the same idea of counting every source.
Why the calculator does not use eight glasses

The calculator describes the eight-glasses rule as an oversimplification. Eight 8 oz glasses is 64 oz, which equals the weight-based baseline of a 128 lb person with a sedentary day in a temperate climate and nothing else added. Anyone heavier, more active or in a hotter place lands above that on this method.

The climate options are broad categories, not live weather. On a day with a high heat index you may need more than the calculator's hot-climate figure, and for outdoor work OSHA says to drink water frequently rather than only when thirsty and to provide electrolyte drinks such as sports drinks on jobs longer than two hours. The CDC advises older adults to drink more water than usual in the heat and not to wait until they are thirsty. The CDC also notes that drinking water can help prevent dehydration, which may cause unclear thinking, mood change, overheating, constipation and kidney stones.

items: Treating the result as a prescription. It is a rule-of-thumb starting point built from three inputs.
Ignoring what you already drink and eat. Count tea, coffee, soups and food moisture before adding more.
Drinking an entire target in one sitting. Spread intake through the day and use thirst and urine color as checks.
Using it for situations it does not model. It has no inputs for age, pregnancy, illness or medications.
Assuming more is always better. Do not push far beyond your thirst without advice from a clinician.

sections.text: If you have kidney, heart or liver disease, have been told to limit fluids, take diuretics or other medicines that affect fluid balance, are pregnant or are caring for a child, ask a clinician for a fluid target instead of relying on this calculator.
